blocks.text: Look at the zebra crossing markings on a road: the white bars are parallel, and the kerb cuts across them all at the same slant. Every angle formed repeats in a pattern. Geometry questions are built on exactly that pattern.

blocks.markdown:
Two facts underpin everything in this subtopic:

- **Angles on a straight line add up to $180°$.** Such angles are called *supplementary*.
- **Angles at a point add up to $360°$**, because a full turn is $360°$.

A third fact, worth remembering separately: two angles adding to $90°$ are *complementary*.

blocks.title: Transversal
blocks.text: A transversal is a line that cuts across two or more other lines. When the lines it cuts are **parallel**, special equal-angle relationships appear, and these are what exam questions test.

blocks.caption: The F, Z and C shapes are the fastest way to identify each pair

blocks.markdown:
### Two are equal, one is supplementary

Corresponding and alternate angles are **equal**. Co-interior angles are **supplementary** — they add to $180°$.

That single distinction is the most common source of lost marks. If two angles are on the *same side* of the transversal and *between* the parallel lines, they add to $180°$; otherwise, on parallel lines, they are equal.

Note that vertically opposite angles are equal whether or not the lines are parallel.

blocks.title: A multi-step angle chase
blocks.prompt: Three angles lie on a straight line and are x, 2x and 3x. Find x, then state the largest angle.

steps.text: Angles on a straight line add to 180°, so form an equation.

blocks.answer: x = 30°, and the largest angle is 90°

Write a reason beside each step, such as "alternate angles" or "angles on a straight line".
Look for the F, Z, C and X shapes before doing any arithmetic.
Check that your final angles are consistent with the whole diagram.

blocks.title: Reasons carry marks
blocks.text: In WAEC and NECO theory papers, stating the reason is worth marks even when the number is already correct. Write "corresponding angles, parallel lines" rather than just "= 70°".

points: Angles on a straight line add to 180°; angles at a point add to 360°.
Vertically opposite angles are always equal.
On parallel lines, corresponding (F) and alternate (Z) angles are equal.
On parallel lines, co-interior (C) angles add to 180°.
Mark known angles on the diagram and give a reason for every step.
Form an equation when angles are given in terms of x, then solve.
